title: Growth since 2025 comes from more orders, not bigger orders
finding: Revenue grew 29.5% in 2025 and 20.4% in 2026. Order count grew 26.7% and 28.3%, while average order value changed 2.2% and -6.2%. In 2024 revenue fell 2.8% even though orders rose 7.1%, because AOV fell 9.2%.

title: Revenue is strongly seasonal: September, November and December carry the year
finding: On average, September, November and December produce 43.5% of annual revenue; January and February together produce 6.5%. The pattern is stable across all four years. Monthly margin is volatile (between -18.1% and 27.2%); 2 months were loss-making (Jul 2023, Jan 2024).

title: Profit grew faster than revenue until 2025; margin slipped in 2026 as discounting rose
finding: Margin rose from 10.2% (2023) to 13.4% (2025), then fell to 12.7% in 2026. Over the same years the effective discount rate moved 22.2% -> 18.4% -> 19.9%. Profit growth was 32.7% in 2025 but 14.2% in 2026.

title: Furniture earns almost nothing, and not only because of discounting
finding: Furniture generates 32.3% of revenue but 6.4% of profit (margin 2.5%, vs 17.4% Technology and 17.0% Office Supplies). Its effective discount (20.0%) is the same as the other categories. At the company's discount mix its margin would still be only 4.8%. Even without any discount, Furniture sub-categories earn 19%-27%, against a median of 36% for other sub-categories.

title: Losses are concentrated: three sub-categories account for two-thirds of all losses
finding: Loss-making order lines lose 156.1k in total, equal to 35.3% of the profit earned on profitable lines. Binders, Tables, Machines account for 64.7% of all losses. Binders are profitable overall (14.9% margin) yet lose 38.5k on individual lines, with an effective discount of 38.7%.

title: Central's weak margin is largely associated with its heavier discounting
finding: Central has the lowest margin (7.9%) and the highest effective discount (24.6%). If Central had the company's discount mix, its margin would be 11.3%, closing about 74% of its gap to the company margin (12.5%). West's lead disappears after adjustment (14.9% -> 10.4%), because West discounts least (15.6%).

title: Customer segment is a weak differentiator of profitability
finding: Segment margins range only from 11.5% to 14.0%, and profit per customer from 328 to 403. Consumer is the largest segment (47.0% of profit) because it has the most customers, not because each customer is worth more. Orders per customer are similar (6.1-6.4).

title: Margin leaks are large; high-margin niche products are too small to offset them
finding: 97 products in the top sales quintile are loss-making: they generate 418.2k revenue (18.2% of total) and lose 54.6k. Most are Tables, Chairs, Bookcases, Storage. A further 86 high-sales products earn below the company margin. By contrast, the 385 low-sales products with at least double the company margin generate only 36.2k revenue (1.6%) and 14.1k profit. 3 of the 10 best-selling products earn zero or negative profit.

title: Profit is highly concentrated in a minority of customers
finding: The top 10% of customers generate 57.9% of profit but 30.9% of revenue; the top 20% generate 81.8% of profit. 155 customers (19.6%) are unprofitable over four years, costing 71.2k.

title: Unprofitable customers are mostly deep-discount customers, driven by a few transactions
finding: Among customers whose effective discount is 30% or more, 84% are unprofitable; among those below 10%, 0% are. The rank correlation between a customer's effective discount and their margin is -0.81. 103 of the 155 unprofitable customers would be profitable if their single worst order line were removed.

title: Repeat buyers carry the business; frequency adds volume, not margin
finding: Customers with 7-10 orders are 38.8% of customers but earn 50.1% of profit. Margin is similar for all bands with 4+ orders (12.3%-12.9%); customers with 1-3 orders earn only 5.2%. The median gap between a customer's orders is 128 days. Year-to-year retention rose from 73.4% to 87.4%.

title: Every loss-making state is a heavy-discount state
finding: 10 states are loss-making, together losing 98.2k on 30.7% of revenue. All of them have an effective discount of at least 29.7%. Across the 28 states with 30+ orders, the rank correlation between effective discount and margin is -0.87. Texas is the 3rd-largest state by revenue but the largest loss (-25.7k, discount 39.1%).

title: City losses concentrate in a few large cities, but city data is thin
finding: 138 cities are loss-making (104.9k in total). The five largest loss cities account for 43.0% of city-level losses, led by Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; Houston, Texas; San Antonio, Texas. Only 14 of 604 cities have 30+ orders.

title: Margin falls steadily with discount; at 30% and above, order lines almost always lose money
finding: Margin is 29.5% at no discount and 11.8% at 20%, then negative at every level from 30% upward. At 30%+ discount, 96.8% of lines lose money; these lines are 13.9% of all lines but produce -135.4k profit. The rank correlation between discount and line margin is -0.64.

title: There is no evidence that discounts increase the volume of each sale
finding: The rank correlation between discount and units per line is 0.00, and between discount and line revenue -0.06. Within the same sub-category, discounted lines carry fewer units than full-price lines in 12 of 17 sub-categories.

title: Discount is set by a fixed rule (state x sub-category), so it is a controllable policy
finding: In all 656 state x sub-category combinations, every order line has exactly the same discount (100% of combinations). State alone explains 50% of the variation in discount, sub-category 26%, and the two together 100%. 11 states never sell at full price; 21 states always do. Storage, Supplies, Tables lose money even at 1-20% discount.
